summary:
Scan from the back of the queue, keeping a Fenwick tree (binary indexed tree) of the heights already seen. For
each person, a prefix-sum query counts the seen heights below theirs, then their height is added. Heights lie
in −10⁴..10⁴, so the tree is small and each step is O(log R). (Merge sort on indices also works.)

question.md:
For every person, count the people **behind** them who are **strictly shorter**.

- **Heights repeat** and can be negative (−10⁴ to 10⁴).
- **Up to 10⁵ people**, so O(n²) is too slow.

think.md:
Heights `[5, 2, 6, 1, 3]` give counts `[3, 1, 2, 0, 0]`: the 5 has 2, 1 and 3 behind it, all shorter.

This is inversion counting, but **per element**. Two ways to get it fast:

- Merge sort the positions by height and credit each left-half person with the right-half people placed before
  them.
- Or walk from the back keeping a running tally of heights seen; each person asks "how many heights in the tally
  are smaller than mine?" A Fenwick tree over the small height range answers that in O(log R).

idea.md: For each `i`, count `j > i` with `heights[j] < heights[i]`.

lines.text: Everyone behind person `i` who is strictly shorter.

walk.title: For each person, look at everyone behind and count the shorter ones.

limits.md: 5 × 10⁹ comparisons for 10⁵ people. The counts are per-element inversions, which merge sort or a tally of heights can produce in O(n log n).

approaches.title: Merge sort on positions

idea.md: Merge sort an array of positions, ordered by height. During a merge, when a person from the left half is placed, every right-half person placed before them is shorter and stands behind them: add `j − mid` to that person's count.

build: Merge sort `idx` by `heights[idx]`, taking from the right only when strictly shorter.
When taking from the left, add `j − mid` to `out[idx[i]]`.

lines.text: Counts, the positions to sort, and a buffer. Sorting positions (not heights) lets each count go to the right person.
Sort each half of the positions by height.
Take a right-half person first only when strictly shorter.
When a left-half person is placed, the `j − mid` right-half people already taken are shorter and stand behind them.
Finish with the remaining right-half people and copy back.

steps.text: Merge positions 0..1: each left person gains the number of right people already taken (shorter).
Merge positions 3..4: each left person gains the number of right people already taken (shorter).
Merge positions 2..4: each left person gains the number of right people already taken (shorter).
Merge positions 0..4: each left person gains the number of right people already taken (shorter).

walk.title: Merge sort the positions by height. When a left-half person is placed, every right-half person already placed is shorter and behind them.

limits.md: Correct, but juggling an index array through the merge is fiddly. With heights in a small range, a tally of seen heights (a Fenwick tree) answers each person's question directly, in a simple loop.

approaches.title: Fenwick tree over heights, from the back

idea.md: Shift heights to 1..R (R = 20001). Walk from the last person to the first: `out[i] = prefix(h[i] − 1)` counts seen heights strictly below, then `add(h[i], 1)`.

build: From the back: query the prefix just below the height, then add the height.

lines.text: A Fenwick tree over the 20,001 possible heights (shifted so −10⁴ becomes 1).
From the back of the queue: the tree holds exactly the people behind person `i`.
Prefix sum up to `h − 1`: how many people behind are strictly shorter. `k & −k` is the lowest set bit, the size of the range each tree cell covers.
Now person `i` is behind everyone further forward: add their height.

complexity.md: **Time O(n log R)** with R = 20,001. **Space O(R).**

steps.text: 3: 0 of the heights behind are smaller. Add 3 to the tally.
1: 0 of the heights behind are smaller. Add 1 to the tally.
6: 2 of the heights behind are smaller. Add 6 to the tally.
2: 1 of the heights behind are smaller. Add 2 to the tally.
5: 3 of the heights behind are smaller. Add 5 to the tally.

walk.title: Walk from the back with a tally of heights seen so far (a Fenwick tree): each person asks how many seen heights are smaller.

takeaways.md:
- **Per-element inversion counts:** merge sort on indices, or a Fenwick tree over values scanned from one end.
- A Fenwick tree gives prefix counts and point updates in O(log R); shift values so they start at 1.
- With large values, compress them to ranks first; the Fenwick approach still works.
